about: What the CipherHorizon inventory scripts collect. Each signature names one read-only capability of the script engine and its parameters; the server interprets what comes back. Edit this file to collect something new: the engines do not change.

signatures.title: Certificates in the Windows certificate stores
signatures.why: Server, client and CA certificates, with their keys' algorithms and expiry; and whether Windows holds a private key for each (the key itself is never read).

signatures.title: TLS and SSL versions set for Windows (Schannel)
signatures.why: IIS, Remote Desktop, SQL Server and .NET use Schannel: a version explicitly enabled or disabled here applies to all of them.

signatures.title: Ciphers and hashes set for Windows (Schannel)
signatures.why: Old ciphers (RC4, DES, 3DES) and hashes (MD5, SHA-1) explicitly enabled or disabled for every Schannel program.

signatures.title: Cipher suite order set on this machine (Schannel)
signatures.why: The suites Windows offers, in order, when an administrator has set them; empty means the Windows default.

signatures.title: Cipher suite order set by Group Policy (Schannel)
signatures.why: A suite order and curve list pushed by Group Policy override the local order.

signatures.title: .NET Framework TLS settings
signatures.why: Without these, older .NET applications may still use TLS 1.0.

signatures.title: Cryptographic libraries installed with applications
signatures.why: Applications that ship their own OpenSSL, NSS, libsodium or similar: their version decides which algorithms they can use, post-quantum ones included.

signatures.title: Installed programs that bring their own cryptography
signatures.why: OpenSSL, OpenSSH, PuTTY, GnuPG and similar, as Windows lists them under installed programs.

signatures.title: OpenSSH server algorithms (Windows)
signatures.why: The key exchange, ciphers, MACs and host key types the built-in OpenSSH server is set to accept.

signatures.title: OpenSSH server host key types (Windows)
signatures.why: The public half of each host key says which signature algorithm clients verify the server with.

signatures.title: Installed cryptographic packages
signatures.why: OpenSSL, GnuTLS, NSS, libgcrypt, OpenSSH and similar, with versions: the version decides which algorithms they can use, post-quantum ones included.

signatures.title: Certificate files in the usual places
signatures.why: Trust stores and the certificates web, mail and proxy servers are configured with. Only CERTIFICATE blocks leave the machine; key directories and key files are never opened.

signatures.title: OpenSSH server algorithms
signatures.why: The key exchange, ciphers, MACs and host key types the SSH server is set to accept, including post-quantum hybrids.

signatures.title: OpenSSH server host key types
signatures.why: The public half of each host key says which signature algorithm clients verify the server with.

signatures.title: OpenSSL system-wide TLS defaults
signatures.why: The minimum protocol, cipher string and groups every program using the system OpenSSL starts from.

signatures.title: System cryptographic policy (RHEL, Fedora)
signatures.why: One setting (DEFAULT, LEGACY, FUTURE, FIPS) that sets the algorithms every system library allows.
